Professor Meeting Notes

Trust-Aware Online Nash Social Welfare Allocation — updated with the latest 2,000-round Frank-Wolfe results.

One-sentence story:
Online Nash Social Welfare allocation can lose legitimate welfare when malicious agents manipulate reported valuations. The current system uses Algorithm 1 as the active trust gate, strongly protects welfare for Byzantine and Burst attacks, and uses count-free Moradi graph decisions as a shadow signal that identifies stealth attacks missed by the active gate.

What you should accomplish in the meeting

What to show

  • You understand the research story from the original draft.
  • You understand what the current code actually does.
  • You can explain why Algorithm 1 helps in some attacks and fails in others.
  • You know that Moradi is currently a detector signal, not yet a welfare-improving allocation mechanism.

What to ask

  • Should the paper be framed as trust-aware online NSW under strategic valuation reports?
  • Should the next step use Moradi as a hard gate, soft risk score, or both?
  • Which application should anchor the paper: cloud resource allocation, wireless/IoT sharing, or abstract online allocation?
Important boundary: do not say “Moradi improves NSW” yet. The current run shows that Moradi labels cover stealth attacks. It does not show a causal welfare effect because Moradi is still outside the allocation loop.

Project from beginning to end

  1. Clean online allocation setting. At each round, one unit of resource arrives. Agents report valuations. The allocator must divide the resource immediately.
  2. Objective. Measure Nash Social Welfare over legitimate agents. Because NSW is a geometric mean, a high score requires useful allocation and balanced legitimate utility.
  3. Problem. The allocator reacts to reported valuations. Malicious agents can inflate, suppress, or strategically time reports to win resource while not contributing to legitimate welfare.
  4. First defense. Import Algorithm 1 from trustworthy consensus as a trust gate. Each legitimate observer accumulates beta evidence and flags agents whose beta gap crosses xi_t.
  5. Integration. Aggregate local Algorithm 1 detections by majority vote to create a global trusted set. Run online NSW allocation only over that trusted set.
  6. Main finding. The active gate protects welfare when attacks create a growing trust gap, but fails when stealth attackers keep beta gap below threshold.
  7. Next idea. Moradi graph signal combines trust and report similarity, so it may detect hidden attackers that avoid Algorithm 1. The research decision is how to connect that signal to allocation.

What the inherited paper draft is trying to do

The draft combines two large ideas: online Nash Social Welfare allocation and trust-based malicious-agent detection. The draft’s broad claim is not just “run NSW,” but “run online NSW in an adversarial environment where the trusted set is learned over time.”

Online NSW side

Provides the allocation objective, online setting, fairness-efficiency motivation, and offline benchmark.

Trustworthy consensus side

Provides beta accumulation, threshold xi_t, and the idea that agents can learn trustworthy neighborhoods from stochastic observations.

Moradi side

Provides a graph detector: combine trust affinity and report-history similarity, then identify a low-degree suspicious minority.

All values are final-round means across 10 trials. Plus-minus values are 95% confidence intervals. The full-horizon offline NSW is 39.039 ± 0.120 for each focused attack because the same legitimate valuation data and seed schedule define the benchmark.

What works: Algorithm 1 detects all malicious agents under Byzantine and Burst with zero final false-positive rate. Welfare is much higher than no-detection.
What fails: Algorithm 1 records zero final detection for Reputation Poison and Trust Mimicry. Their welfare remains essentially unchanged relative to the no-detection run.

Measured effect of the active gate

The active gate changes welfare only when it changes eligibility. Byzantine NSW rises by 97.4% and Burst NSW rises by 46.0% because Algorithm 1 reaches final detection rate 1.000. Reputation Poison and Trust Mimicry barely change because Algorithm 1 finishes at detection rate 0.000.

Main interpretation: the current implementation establishes both the value and limitation of Algorithm 1. It protects NSW when malicious behavior creates a detectable trust gap. It stops helping when adaptive attacks stay below the threshold.

Where the project currently stands

Ready to present

  • A complete pipeline from strategic reports through trust detection and online NSW allocation to legitimate welfare metrics.
  • A 2,000-round, 10-trial evaluation with every-round means and 95% confidence intervals.
  • A direct no-detection baseline showing when the active gate changes welfare and when it does not.
  • Count-free online Moradi evidence for all four focused attacks, including stealth attacks missed by Algorithm 1.
  • Sensitivity results for attacker count, alpha, sigma, prediction scenarios, and compound attack.

Claim boundary

  • Do claim: Algorithm 1 protects welfare against attacks that create a growing trust gap.
  • Do claim: stealth attacks reveal a limitation of threshold-only trust gating.
  • Do claim: Moradi has detector coverage over attacks missed by Algorithm 1.
  • Do not claim: Moradi improves NSW allocation yet.
  • Do not claim: this is a final theoretical unification of NSW and trustworthy consensus.

Recommended next experiment

Keep the same four focused attacks, seeds, 2,000-round horizon, and Frank-Wolfe benchmark. Change only how the Moradi signal enters allocation.

Questions to ask the professor

  1. Is “trust-aware online NSW under strategic valuation reports” the right primary framing?
  2. Should Moradi be evaluated as a hard detector, a soft risk signal, or both?
  3. Is it acceptable to keep Algorithm 1 as the hard gate while applying Moradi only to the greedy allocation component?
  4. Should the final experimental section stay focused on Byzantine, Burst, Reputation Poison, and Trust Mimicry?
  5. Which application should anchor the paper: cloud resource allocation, wireless/IoT resource sharing, or a more abstract online allocation setting?
  6. What false-positive and welfare criteria should determine whether Moradi is safe enough to enter the allocation loop?

Two-minute meeting script

My project connects online Nash Social Welfare allocation with trust-based detection from trustworthy consensus. In each round, agents report valuations and the allocator immediately divides one unit of resource. The objective measures the geometric mean of legitimate-agent utilities, so the system needs both efficient allocation and a reasonable utility floor.

The problem is that malicious agents can manipulate their reports and continue competing for allocation. The current code uses Algorithm 1 as the active trust gate. Each legitimate observer accumulates beta trust evidence, compares agents with a growing threshold xi_t, and majority voting creates the trusted set used by the online NSW allocator.

In the current 2,000-round, 10-trial run, this gate detects all malicious agents under Byzantine and Burst attacks. Relative to the no-detection baseline, legitimate NSW rises by 97.4% for Byzantine and 46.0% for Burst. The allocation heatmap confirms the mechanism: malicious allocation collapses once the gate flags them.

The limitation appears under Reputation Poison and Trust Mimicry. Their beta gaps stay below the Algorithm 1 threshold, so final detection is zero and legitimate NSW is essentially unchanged from the no-detection run.

I also evaluate a count-free Moradi graph every 20 rounds. It combines trust with report similarity and reaches F1 equal to one for all four focused attacks, including the two stealth attacks. It is still a shadow detector, so I am not claiming that it improves welfare yet.

The decision I want to discuss is the next integration step. I can test Moradi as a second hard gate, or use its score as a soft risk weight on the greedy half of allocation. I prefer to test both, starting with the soft version because it limits false-positive damage.

Honest limitations

  • Full connectivity and full trust observation simplify the setting relative to sparse or intermittent networks.
  • The offline benchmark sees the complete 2,000-round sequence, while the online allocator acts without future information.
  • The intermediate online-to-offline curve is progress toward a full-horizon benchmark, not a prefix competitive ratio.
  • Reputation Poison and Trust Mimicry are adaptive stress tests and may extend beyond the assumptions used to prove the original trust result.
  • Moradi F1 does not establish a welfare effect until Moradi changes eligibility or allocation weights.
  • The first-hit round is not enough to establish stable convergence; persistence and recovery should be reported in the next detector-integration experiment.
  • The prediction-scenario stress test uses eight trials per scenario, while focused attacks and displayed sweeps use 10 trials.
Current conclusion: the current results establish a complete trust-aware online NSW baseline and identify the exact point where the active detector stops helping. Algorithm 1 protects welfare against attacks that create a growing trust gap. Moradi supplies promising detector evidence for stealth attacks, but the next experiment must connect that signal to allocation before making any welfare claim about Moradi.
